name: Walter Irvin
bio: Walter Irvin was one of the Groveland Four, young Black men accused of raping a white woman in Lake County, Florida in 1949 in a case built on coerced confessions and mob terror. Convicted by an all-white jury and sentenced to death, he won a new trial from the U.S. Supreme Court; while Sheriff Willis McCall was transporting him and Samuel Shepherd, handcuffed, in November 1951, McCall shot them both, killing Shepherd and gravely wounding Irvin, then claimed an escape attempt. Irvin survived, was reconvicted and again sentenced to death, later commuted to life; he was paroled in 1968 and posthumously exonerated decades later.
charges: Rape of a white woman in Groveland, Florida (1949) — a capital conviction by an all-white jury on coerced confessions, the Civil Rights Congress's emblematic racial frame-up.
convicted: Convicted and sentenced to death; conviction reversed by the Supreme Court (1951), reconvicted at retrial; death sentence commuted to life.
sentence: Death, later commuted to life; paroled 1968. Shot and wounded by Sheriff McCall while handcuffed in 1951.

name: Samuel Shepherd
bio: Samuel Shepherd was one of the Groveland Four, convicted by an all-white Florida jury of a 1949 rape and sentenced to death in a case the Civil Rights Congress denounced as a racial frame-up. After the U.S. Supreme Court reversed his conviction, Sheriff Willis McCall shot him dead on November 6, 1951 while transporting him and Walter Irvin, handcuffed together, to a hearing — claiming the prisoners had tried to escape.
charges: Rape of a white woman in Groveland, Florida (1949) — a capital conviction by an all-white jury on coerced confessions.
convicted: Convicted and sentenced to death; conviction reversed by the U.S. Supreme Court in 1951.
sentence: Death; killed by Sheriff Willis McCall on November 6, 1951 while handcuffed, before his retrial.

name: Charles Greenlee
bio: Charles Greenlee was the youngest of the Groveland Four — sixteen at the time — convicted in the 1949 Lake County, Florida rape case that became a national symbol of Jim Crow injustice. Spared the death penalty because of his age, he was sentenced to life imprisonment; he was paroled in 1962 and, with the others, posthumously pardoned in 2019 and exonerated in 2021.
charges: Rape of a white woman in Groveland, Florida (1949) — convicted as a 16-year-old by an all-white jury on coerced confessions.
convicted: Convicted; sentenced to life imprisonment (spared death due to his age).
sentence: Life imprisonment; paroled 1962. Posthumously pardoned (2019) and exonerated (2021).

name: Sang Ryup Park
bio: Sang Ryup Park was an editor of the Los Angeles Korean Independence News, a newspaper favoring a unified, independent Korea, ordered deported under the McCarran Act amid the Korean War. He won a last-minute stay in late 1951 against deportation to South Korea, where supporters warned he faced death for his political views.
charges: Deportation under the McCarran Act — as a Korean independence editor opposing the U.S.-backed South Korean regime.
convicted: Ordered deported; won a last-minute stay (December 1951).
sentence: Deportation order stayed; faced death if returned to South Korea.

name: Diamond Kim
bio: Diamond Kim (Kim Kang) was the chief editor of the Los Angeles Korean Independence News, advocating a unified, independent Korea. He was arrested for deportation under the McCarran Act ten days before the Korean War began, targeted for his opposition to the U.S.-backed Syngman Rhee government.
charges: Deportation under the McCarran Act — as a Korean independence editor opposing the South Korean regime.
sentence: Detention and deportation proceedings; faced death if returned to South Korea.

name: Martin Young
bio: Martin Young was a labor organizer (Transport Workers Union and Steelworkers) arrested on October 26, 1951 and held without bail at Ellis Island under the McCarran Act — reportedly the only McCarran detainee so held, and confined among mentally ill inmates — facing deportation for his alleged Communist affiliation.
charges: Deportation under the McCarran Act for alleged Communist affiliation.
convicted: Arrested October 1951; held without bail at Ellis Island.

name: Abdel Mohsen Hamouda
bio: Abdel Mohsen Hamouda was an Egyptian in Denver arrested without a warrant on November 30, 1951 and held incommunicado in solitary confinement, denied medical care, after speaking publicly against a proposed British–U.S. Middle East military pact — a political arrest tied to his anti-colonial views.
charges: Immigration arrest / detention — following a political speech against a British–U.S. Middle East pact.
convicted: Arrested without warrant and held incommunicado (November 1951).

name: Willie Thomas
bio: Willie Thomas was a Black man held in Albany, New York in 1951 for extradition back to an Alabama chain gang, from which he had escaped years after being sentenced to life at age fourteen for a robbery. The Civil Rights Congress campaigned to block his return after Governor Dewey signed the extradition papers.
charges: Fugitive from an Alabama chain gang (a life sentence imposed at age 14 for robbery) — facing extradition.
convicted: Originally convicted in Alabama as a child; fought 1951 extradition from New York.
sentence: Life on an Alabama chain gang; subject of a CRC anti-extradition campaign.

name: Israel Amter
bio: Israel Amter was a veteran New York Communist leader — long the face of the Party's unemployed and street-organizing campaigns — who, at about seventy and in poor health, was among the seventeen 'second-string' Communist leaders arrested in New York on June 20, 1951 under the Smith Act.
charges: Smith Act — conspiring to advocate the overthrow of the government (New York second-string roundup).
convicted: Arrested June 20, 1951; tried with the New York Smith Act group.
sentence: Prosecuted under the Smith Act (charges affected by later Yates ruling).

name: William Weinstone
bio: William Weinstone was a founding-generation American Communist leader arrested in New York on June 20, 1951 as one of the seventeen 'second-string' Party leaders charged under the Smith Act.
charges: Smith Act — conspiring to advocate the overthrow of the government (New York second-string roundup).
convicted: Arrested June 20, 1951; tried with the New York Smith Act group.
sentence: Prosecuted under the Smith Act (charges affected by later Yates ruling).

name: Vincent Hallinan
bio: Vincent Hallinan was a combative San Francisco trial lawyer who defended longshore leader Harry Bridges in his 1949–50 denaturalization and perjury trial. For his aggressive courtroom defense, Judge George Harris jailed him for contempt of court; the Supreme Court declined to review, and Hallinan served six months — after which he ran for President in 1952 on the Progressive Party ticket.
charges: Contempt of court — for his defense of Harry Bridges in the government's denaturalization/perjury case.
convicted: Convicted of contempt; the Supreme Court denied review.
